suggestions.title: 7-day prep plan
suggestions.reason: A day-by-day plan so the week before the interview is structured instead of last-minute

content.text: Interview prep: 7-day plan
Goal: walk in knowing the company, with 6-8 rehearsed stories, sharp technical fundamentals, and good questions to ask.
Days 7-6: Research and foundations
Re-read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Fill in the Company research page (product, model, competitors, regulation)
Look up each interviewer on LinkedIn and note common ground
Days 5-3: Stories and technical practice
Write 6-8 STAR stories in the Story bank table
Do 2 timed practice problems per day (see Technical practice tracker)
Review payments, ledger and compliance basics (KYC/AML, PCI, settlement)
Days 2-1: Mock interviews and logistics
Do one full mock interview out loud, with a friend or recorded
Finalize the 'Tell me about yourself' pitch (under 90 seconds)
Test camera, mic, video link and internet, or plan the route and arrival time
Pick the outfit and print or save copies of your resume
Interview day
Light review of stories only; no new cramming
Send a thank-you email within 24 hours

suggestions.title: Fintech concepts cheat sheet
suggestions.reason: A quick-reference of domain concepts that commonly come up in fintech interviews

content.text: Fintech concepts cheat sheet
Payments flow
Authorization, capture, clearing, settlement. Know who the issuer, acquirer, processor and card network are, and where fees (interchange) are taken.
Ledgers and money movement
Double-entry bookkeeping: every transaction has balanced debits and credits
Idempotency keys, retries, and reconciliation of internal vs. bank records
Use integers or decimals for money, never floats
Compliance and risk
KYC / AML: identity verification, sanctions screening, transaction monitoring
PCI-DSS, SOC 2, data encryption, audit trails
Fraud signals, chargebacks, and the trade-off between false positives and losses
Metrics to know
TPV (total payment volume), take rate, CAC / LTV, churn, default rate, net revenue retention.

suggestions.title: Questions to ask them
suggestions.reason: Strong closing questions signal genuine interest and help you evaluate the role

content.text: Questions to ask interviewers
About the role
What would success look like in the first 90 days?
What is the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?
About the company and regulation
How do compliance and regulatory requirements shape the product roadmap?
How does the team balance shipping speed with risk controls?
About the team and culture
How are decisions made and how does the team handle disagreement?
What does career growth look like for someone in this role?
Next steps: ask about the timeline and what happens after this round.

content.text: Launch content campaign: 6-week brief
Product launch is 14 November 2026 (moved because the payments review slipped). The campaign runs 12 Oct to 22 Nov 2026, with the launch landing in week 5. Team: Sam, Priya, Alex.
Goal
Turn launch attention into qualified demo requests and trial signups. Set the numeric targets with the team in the first check-in and track them on the Results table.
Phases
Weeks 1-2 (12-25 Oct): Tease. Problem-led blog posts, LinkedIn thought leadership, waitlist email.
Weeks 3-4 (26 Oct-8 Nov): Build. Demo video, podcast appearances, press embargo outreach, early-access emails.
Week 5 (9-15 Nov): Launch. Press release, launch email, webinar, LinkedIn push on 14 Nov.
Week 6 (16-22 Nov): Sustain. Customer stories, recap content, retargeting, results review.
Audience
Decision makers and hands-on evaluators at B2B teams who feel the pain the product solves. Write for the evaluator first and give the decision maker a clear business case.
Key messages
The problem is costly and getting worse.
Our product fixes it faster than the status quo, shown in the demo video.
Getting started is easy: self-serve trial with simple payments.
Kick-off checklist
Agree numeric targets for demo requests and signups
Confirm total budget and channel split
Fill the content calendar for weeks 1-3
Set up UTM naming so results are attributable by channel
Book the weekly 30-minute check-in

Hi team,

Thanks for making time for the Plexii Pulse kickoff. Here is a quick summary of what we are aiming for, when things happen, and who is driving each piece, so we all start from the same page.

What we are trying to achieve

  • Give customers a clear reason to try it, backed by launch messaging, documentation, and in-product guidance that are ready on day one.
  • Have support and sales prepared, so that every question in the first two weeks gets a fast and consistent answer.
  • Set up measurement before launch, so we can judge adoption and quality from the first day.

Timeline

The plan runs for eight weeks, with a review at the end of each phase. If a date is at risk, tell me early so we can adjust together.

verdict.reason: The agenda adds up to exactly 45 minutes (5+10+7+7+7+7+2) and gives each item a lead and an outcome, with no invented specifics beyond sensible template defaults; the decision criteria, the 48-hour follow-up and the one-hour minutes rule are the assistant's own proposals rather than facts, and the extra sections make it slightly longer than a concise one-pager needs.

results.text:
Launch Readiness Meeting

This 45 minute session exists to decide whether the launch goes ahead on the planned date. Every workstream lead should arrive ready to give a clear status of green, amber or red, and to name any open risk that could change the decision.

Date and timeFacilitatorNote takerLocation or link
    

Agenda

TimeTopicLeadOutcome needed
0:00 to 0:05Welcome, launch goal and success criteriaFacilitatorShared understanding of what "ready" means today
0:05 to 0:15Product and engineering readiness, including feature completeness, performance and infrastructureEngineering leadConfirmed status and list of any open blockers
0:15 to 0:22Quality review, covering test results, open defects and security checksQA leadAgreement on which defects are acceptable at launch
0:22 to 0:29Go-to-market and support readiness, including messaging, documentation, training and staffingMarketing and support leadsConfirmation that customers and the support team are prepared
0:29 to 0:36Launch day plan, monitoring and rollbackRelease managerAgreed sequence, owners and rollback trigger
0:36 to 0:43Risk review and go or no-go decisionExecutive sponsorA recorded decision: go, go with conditions, or delay
0:43 to 0:45Action items and closeNote takerEvery action has an owner and a due date

Before the meeting

  • Each workstream lead updates the readiness tracker with a green, amber or red status by end of day before the meeting.
  • QA shares the latest test summary and the open defect list, sorted by severity.
  • The release manager circulates the draft launch day runbook so attendees can review it in advance.

How the decision will be made

A go decision requires no red items, no open critical or high severity defects, and a tested rollback plan. Amber items are acceptable only if they have a named owner and a mitigation in place before launch. If these conditions are not met, the sponsor will either set conditions with a deadline or move the launch date, and the group will agree on a follow-up check within 48 hours.

Ground rules

  • Status updates stay within their time slot, and deeper problems move to a separate session after the meeting.
  • Raise risks early and plainly, even if they are uncomfortable.
  • Decisions and actions are recorded live and sent to all attendees within one hour of the meeting ending.

results.prompt: Write a short FAQ about our refund policy: full refund within 30 days, no refunds after that, annual plans refunded pro rata.

verdict.reason: The FAQ invents terms beyond the policy: no reason is needed, access continues until period end, refunds cover full months only, a $120 example, an email request process, refunds go to the original payment method, and access ends when the refund is processed. It also contradicts the given policy by saying refunds are 'not offered on monthly plans' after 30 days and by stating annual plans are refunded pro rata only after the 30 days.

results.text:
Refund Policy FAQ

Can I get a refund if I change my mind?

Yes. If you ask for a refund within 30 days of your purchase, we will refund the full amount. You do not need to give a reason.

What happens after the 30 days are up?

Once the 30-day window has closed, we do not offer refunds on monthly plans. You can cancel at any time to stop future charges, and you will keep access until the end of the period you have already paid for.

How do refunds work for annual plans?

Key findings:

Browsers are the dominant memory cost and the main stability risk. Each live browser is a separate Chromium renderer that never sleeps, so offscreen or hidden browsers still consume full CPU and memory. Heavy SPAs push a single browser to 150-400 MB, and beyond roughly 9-15 browsers on one desk the app faces swap pressure, compositor jank, and possible renderer kills.

The canvas has no viewport culling, so every widget on the active desk is fully mounted and live whether visible or not. This makes pan and zoom expensive on busy desks, especially with browsers.

Live wires are the main CPU hot path during interaction. The wire overlay recomputes bounding rectangles for every wire on every animation frame during a drag, which becomes choppy beyond roughly 30-50 wires. The minimap, which re-renders every widget as a live preview, is the second hot path on dense desks.

Non-browser widgets are cheap individually. Most use little memory, and the app stays responsive for typical desks of up to about 60 such widgets.

Top 3 recommendations:

1. Suspend offscreen and hidden browsers. Use an IntersectionObserver or pan/zoom visibility check in the web view widget to mute, freeze, or unload browsers that are far off screen, reloading them when they return. This removes most of the memory and stability risk.

2. Viewport-cull the canvas. Skip mounting widgets well outside the visible area, with a margin, so large desks only mount what is near view. This mainly helps browsers and reduces pan and zoom jank.

3. Soft-cap and warn on browsers per desk. Track the live browser count and show a gentle performance hint past about 8 browsers on one desk, preventing the most common surprise failures without a hard limit.

verdict.reason: Accurately and concisely states the phased hybrid decision, the rejected Option B, and all five listed risks with mitigations, with nothing invented.

results.text:
**Decision:** Adopt a phased hybrid rather than replacing the `<webview>`. Phase 1 (shipped) hardens the existing `<webview>`: clean UA, overlay `setActive` instead of `focusOn`, origin-gated autofill, and a permission denylist. Phase 2 (proposed) adds an external-browser OAuth handoff via `shell.openExternal` and `haptyx://` for providers that block embedded browsers. Phase 3 (proposed) adds a `WebContentsView` in the focus/expand surface, with `session.loadExtension` for a vetted shelf (uBlock-Lite, Dark Reader). Phase 4 (proposed, spike-gated) uses a screenshot at rest plus one pooled native view on activate. Option B, a wholesale native `WebContentsView` migration, is rejected because it would sacrifice smooth pan/zoom, clipping and layering, which are the product's signature feel [1].

**Main risks listed:**
- UA regex mangling the version string. This is mitigated by unit tests and idempotency [1].
- Some enterprise SSO blocks embedded browsers regardless of UA. Only Phase 2 fixes this; Phase 1 narrows the failure set but does not eliminate it [1].
- Phase 4's native-view/CSS-transform sync is make-or-break. It needs a spike proving 60fps tracking and acceptable clipping; if the spike fails, stop at Phase 3 [1].
- The origin gate may be too strict for edge-case login domains. It fails closed, so autofill simply doesn't fire [1].
- Extension security. Use a vetted shelf only, load specific reviewed builds, never arbitrary user extensions, and document the supported API subset [1].

The ADR also cautions against marketing "any Chrome plugin", since Electron supports only a subset of the extension API [1].

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

Our team wiki has grown over several years into a mix of current guidance, outdated pages, and duplicated notes. Finding the right answer often depends on knowing who to ask rather than where to look. This project moves the wiki into PlexiiWrite and uses the move as a chance to clean up what we carry over, so that the new workspace is easier to trust and easier to maintain from day one.
Goals
The migration should leave us with a single, searchable home for team knowledge that people actually prefer to use. Success means the following outcomes are met within 60 days of launch.
All pages identified as active are available in PlexiiWrite with working links, images, and attachments.
Every migrated section has a named owner responsible for keeping it current.
Search returns the correct page for the 20 most common team questions, tested before launch.
The old wiki is set to read-only and then retired, with no team members still editing it.
Weekly active use in PlexiiWrite matches or exceeds use of the old wiki within two months.
Scope

In scope is the full content audit of the existing wiki, migration of pages judged worth keeping, a new top-level structure and naming convention, page templates for recurring document types such as runbooks and meeting notes, permission setup, and a short training session for the team.

Out of scope are rewriting content that is accurate but merely inelegant, migrating archived project material that has not been touched in over two years (this will be exported to cold storage instead), and integrations with other tools beyond basic link redirects. These can be considered as a follow-on phase once the core migration is stable.
Timeline
The project runs about six weeks from kickoff to retirement of the old wiki.
Week 1: Audit existing pages, tag each as keep, update, or archive, and assign section owners.
Week 2: Design the new structure, templates, and permissions in PlexiiWrite, and review them with the team.
Weeks 3 and 4: Migrate content in batches by section, with owners checking their own pages for broken formatting and links.
Week 5: Run search tests, fix gaps, hold the training session, and announce the cutover date.
Week 6: Cut over, set the old wiki to read-only, and collect feedback. Retire the old wiki at the end of the following month if no blockers appear.
Risks and Mitigations

The largest risk is that owners treat migration as a low priority and leave pages half-reviewed. To reduce this, each owner receives a fixed list of pages and a deadline in week 4, and progress is reviewed in the weekly team meeting.
Formatting loss is likely for tables, embedded files, and internal links. We will migrate a small pilot section first to learn what breaks, then adjust the process before moving the rest.

People may keep using the old wiki out of habit, which would split our knowledge across two places. A clear cutover date, an early read-only switch, and redirect notices on the old pages should prevent this.

Finally, permissions can be misconfigured during setup, exposing sensitive pages or locking out the people who need them. We will define access groups during week 2 and have a second person verify them before any content is moved.
Roles and Next Steps

A project lead will coordinate the schedule and own communication with the team. slides.title: The Neighbourhood Tool Library
slides.notes: Welcome everyone and thank you for coming. Tonight I want to show you a simple idea that could save our street money, clutter and a lot of unnecessary shopping trips.

slides.title: We all own tools we barely use
bullets: The average power drill is used for about 13 minutes in its lifetime
Most homes hold hundreds of dollars of tools that sit idle
Buying for a single job is expensive and wasteful
Garages and sheds fill up while projects still stall
New neighbours and renters often have no tools at all
slides.notes: Start with something everyone recognises: the drill in the cupboard that comes out twice a year. Point out that this is a cost problem, a space problem and a fairness problem, since not everyone can afford to buy what a repair needs.

slides.title: A shared shelf that works like a library
bullets: Neighbours borrow tools for free or for a small annual fee
Items are checked out for a week, then returned
A simple catalogue shows what is available
Volunteers handle sign-ups, repairs and returns
Donated and surplus tools stock the shelves from day one
slides.notes: Explain that the model is borrowed from book libraries, so people already understand how it works. Keep it concrete: you walk in, borrow a ladder or a sander, and bring it back when the job is done.

slides.title: What it gives the neighbourhood
bullets: Real savings for households on every project
Less waste, because fewer tools are bought and discarded
Skills shared through workshops and repair days
New connections between neighbours who would not otherwise meet
More people able to fix and improve their own homes
slides.notes: This is the heart of the pitch. The savings are easy to measure, but the lasting value is the community that forms around a shared resource. Share a short story if you have one, such as a neighbour helping another learn to hang a shelf.

slides.title: How we get started
bullets: Secure a small space such as a church hall, garage or community centre
Collect donated tools through a neighbourhood drive
Recruit ten volunteers to run opening hours
Launch with a free community repair day
We need your tools, your time or a space to host
slides.notes: Close with a clear, modest ask. We are not building anything huge, we are starting with a shelf, a sign-up sheet and a few willing people. Invite everyone to leave their name and one thing they could give before they go home.
